prompt.context: Our client is a major global airline considering a co-branded credit card with a major bank. They've hired McKinsey to evaluate what the effects of this program would be, and whether or not they should revise their loyalty program to incorporate the co-branded card.
prompt.question: As the airline, what are the benefits and risks you would think about when evaluating the co-branded credit card? Then the interviewer will guide you through pricing the mile and analyzing the impact of a revised frequent flier program.

clarifying_info.q: How is the co-branded card structured?
clarifying_info.a: The bank would purchase batches of miles from the airline to give away as rewards for purchases and promotions.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average purchase amount and purchase frequency for a customer?
clarifying_info.a: The average purchase is about $50 and a customer will make an average of 1,000 purchases per year.

clarifying_info.q: How many points does a customer earn per dollar spent?
clarifying_info.a: For every dollar purchased, a customer gains 1 point.

clarifying_info.q: What do flights cost on average?
What is the exchange rate of points to flights?
What is the probability that a customer will redeem their miles at the end of the year?
What are the current frequent flier tiers?
clarifying_info.a: Member (0–25,000 miles): miles accrue normally. Super Member (25,000–50,000): miles accrue at 25% bonus, free upgrades when available after SAM and SDAM. Super-Awesome Member/SAM (50,000–100,000): miles accrue at 50% bonus, free upgrades after SDAM, president's lounge on international flights, free drink coupons on delays. Super-Duper-Awesome Member/SDAM (>100,000): miles accrue at 75% bonus, free upgrades when available, president's lounge, free drink coupons on delays.

clarifying_info.q: How does the new point system work?
clarifying_info.a: It takes 1,000 miles to gain 1 point. Once a customer reaches a specific level their points reset to zero. It takes 20 points (20,000 miles) to reach Super, 40 additional points (40,000 miles) to reach Super-Awesome, and 60 additional points (60,000 miles) to reach Super-Duper-Awesome.

clarifying_info.q: What is the customer distribution by miles flown?
clarifying_info.a: 0–20,000 miles: 40%; 20,000–25,000 miles: 20% (evenly spread across 20k–50k band); 25,000–50,000 miles: part of the 20% band; 50,000–60,000 miles: 15% (evenly spread across 50k–100k); 60,000–75,000 miles: 7.5%; 75,000–100,000 miles: 4%; 100,000–120,000 miles: 4%; >120,000 miles: remaining ~9.5%.

framework: Benefits of co-branded card: customer acquisition (reach bank depositors/cardholders to expand loyalty base), increased customer loyalty driving more flights and revenue, potential revenue-sharing with credit card company (e.g., percentage of interest payments)

Risks of co-branded card: counterparty concentration risk (reliance on one bank), large overlap between current loyalty customers and bank customers limiting incremental reach, mispricing of miles sold to the credit card company, ambiguity over who bears marketing costs
Pricing framework: derive value of a mile from ticket price, redemption rate (points per flight), annual spend, and redemption probability; price the mile between expected value and face value
Frequent flier program restructure: calculate old vs. new tier distributions using the customer mileage distribution; assess winners and losers; recommend communication and perks strategy
Recommendation: link rewards program design to the most profitable customer segment, not simply the highest-volume flyers

questions.prompt: How would you price a mile to sell to the credit card company?
questions.guidance: Candidate should anchor on the value of a flight, calculate how many miles/points are needed per flight, then derive cost per mile. Must also apply the redemption probability to get expected value. The final price range should be between expected value (2.5 cents) and face value (5 cents).

math.setup: Annual spend = $50 avg purchase × 1,000 purchases = $50,000. Points earned = $50,000 × 1 point/dollar = 50,000 points. Flights redeemable = 50,000 / 10,000 = 5 flights. Retail value of flights = 5 × $500 = $2,500. Face value per point = $2,500 / 50,000 = $0.05 (5 cents). Expected value per point = 5 cents × 50% redemption probability = 2.5 cents.
math.answer: Price a mile between 2.5 cents (expected value) and 5 cents (face/retail value).

questions.prompt: Calculate the percentage of customers in each tier under the old system vs. the new system. What does this mean for the airline?
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a comparison table. For the old system, use the given mileage distribution and interpolate proportionally within bands. For the new system, note that milestones reset: 20,000 miles to Super, then 40,000 more (60,000 cumulative) to SAM, then 60,000 more (120,000 cumulative) to SDAM. Key insight: new system makes Super easier (35% vs. 22.5%) but loses more high-tier members (SDAM 9.5% vs. 13.5%).

math.setup: Customer distribution bands (from exhibit): 0–20k: 40%; 20k–50k: 20% (uniform); 50k–75k: 15% (uniform); 75k–100k: 7.5%; 100k–120k: 4%; >120k: 4% (implied remaining ≈9.5% SDAM old). Old thresholds: Member <25k, Super 25k–50k, SAM 50k–100k, SDAM >100k. New cumulative thresholds: Member <20k, Super 20k–60k, SAM 60k–120k, SDAM >120k.
math.answer: Old: Member 45%, Super 22.5%, SAM 19%, SDAM 13.5%. New: Member 40%, Super 35%, SAM 15.5%, SDAM 9.5%. More customers reach Super under the new system but fewer reach SAM and SDAM — high-volume flyers lose status.

brainstorming.prompt: How might the airline communicate the program changes to customers, and what adjustments could ease the transition?

categories.name: Communication channels
ideas: Personal mailing or phone calls to high-volume SDAM/SAM customers
Incorporate messaging into pre-flight safety videos or in-flight announcements

categories.name: Program adjustments to ease transition
ideas: Grandfather in current customers so they keep whichever tier is higher under old vs. new rules
Increase accrual bonuses at higher tiers to make them more attractive (e.g., 33%, 67%, 80% instead of 25%, 50%, 75%)
Offer a transition grace period during which mile counts are not reset

categories.name: Framing and messaging
ideas: Emphasize that it is now easier to reach Super status
Highlight enhanced or unchanged perks for high-tier members
Be transparent about the reset mechanic to avoid customer confusion

recommendation: The airline should proceed with the co-branded card but price miles carefully between 2.5 and 5 cents, negotiating toward the higher end to capture margin
Revise the loyalty program restructuring to protect high-value customers: consider grandfathering current status and improving accrual bonuses at elite tiers
risks: High-volume SDAM and SAM flyers may defect to competitors if they feel undervalued after losing status under the new system
Mispricing miles too cheaply to the bank erodes the airline's economics and devalues the loyalty currency
Counterparty concentration with a single bank partner creates partnership risk
next_steps: Segment customers by profitability (not just mileage) to ensure program perks are aligned with the highest-margin flyers
Negotiate revenue-sharing and pricing terms with the bank partner
Design grandfathering and communication plan before launch to retain elite members
Test new tier thresholds with a pilot cohort before full rollout
